The effects of load, F(1, 110) = 8.00, p = .006; mood F(1, 110) = 9.83, p = .002; direction, F(1, 110) = 135.31, p < .001; load and mood, F(1, 110) = 10.97, p = .001; load and direction, F(1, 110) = 10.44, p = .002 and mood and direction, F(1, 110) = 4.14, p = .04, were also significant.\n\nFor ease of interpreting the three-way interaction, the pattern of means is presented in Fig. 3, and the cognitive load and no load conditions are analyzed separately, with comparisons to the control condition.5\n\n## No load conditions\nAll participants in the study believed they shared a birthday with the comparison targets; therefore, the positive mood conditions were expected to replicate the positive mood and shared-birthday conditions in Experiment 1.\n\nThe expected asymmetry among positive mood participants was found. Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found, regardless of whether participants upwardly compared (M = 5.64, SD = .78; F(1,124) = 17.39, p < .001) or downwardly compared (M = 5.15, SD = .81), F(1,124) = 11.90, p = .001.\n\nThe neutral mood conditions replicated previous findings of symmetric assimilation (Brown et al. [1992]). Upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.47, SD = .51) than the control condition, F(1,124) = 17.89, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings than the control condition (M = 3.24, SD = 1.09), F(1,124) = 10.37, p = .002.\n\nThus, positive mood led to asymmetric and self-serving responses, whereas neutral mood led to symmetric responses.\n\n## Cognitive load conditions\nCognitive load was expected to disrupt the self-serving processing of participants in a positive mood, leading them to respond in the same manner as those in the neutral mood conditions.\n\nAs expected, cognitive load disrupted the self-serving responding associated with a positive mood. Instead, participants in a positive mood assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21), upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.71, SD = .83), F(1,124) = 23.14, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 3.09, SD = .94), t(124) = -3.30, p = .001. This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition.\n\nExperiment 4 demonstrated that self-serving responding associated with positive mood is resource-dependent. When people in a positive mood were not under additional cognitive load, they adjusted their interpretations of the meaning of a shared birthday and responded to comparison targets in a self-serving ways, replicating Experiments 1 and 2. However, when cognitive resources were reduced, it was more difficult to adjust the interpretation of the meaning of a shared a birthday and, consequently, participants did not respond to comparisons in self-serving ways. Instead, their responses were like those of neutral mood participants: They assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Thus, when cognitive resources were lacking, the benefits of a positive mood were muted.\n\n## General discussion\nIn four studies, positive mood led to self-serving interpretations of ambiguous similarity information. When participants were given ambiguous similarity information, they categorized targets in self-serving ways. If the comparison person was superior, they used the information to make the target distinctively similar, basked in that person\u2019s glory, and boosted their self-evaluations. If the comparison person was inferior, they used the information to make the target either irrelevant or only generally similar, leading to no response to the comparison target or contrast of their self-evaluations with the inferior target. Overall, this pattern of self-serving responding was not found when the preference information was unambiguous or when participants were under cognitive loaded.\n\nThese studies establish that mood can determine how people interpret and respond to comparison information. These studies also revealed boundary conditions to self-serving responding that provide insight into the underlying processes. First, self-serving responses only occurred when individuals were given ambiguous or flexible information about the relation between themselves and a comparison target. In Experiment 1, when individuals were not told that they shared a birthday with the comparison targets, they were unable to respond in a self-serving manner. Likewise, in Experiment 3, when similarity information was unambiguous, they did not respond in a self-serving manner. Thus, while positive mood might provide cognitive flexibility, positive mood does not blind individuals from seeing negative information. In the absence of ambiguous information, self-serving responses did not arise.\n\nSecond, the effect only occurred when individuals had adequate cognitive resources. That cognitive load derailed the self-serving responses suggests that the flexible processing of comparison targets in positive moods is an effortful process and may be a correction process (e.g., Gilbert et al. [1995]; Stapel and Marx [2007]). In Experiment 4, in the absence of adequate cognitive resources, positive mood participants\u2019 responses to the comparison targets were similar to the responses to neutral mood participants. That is, they were unable to make corrections or engage in reinterpretation of ambiguous information in order to avoid assimilation to the downward comparison target. This supports our suggestion of a two-step process in which individuals in a positive mood initially respond to social comparison information in a consistent manner, and only engage in effortful reanalysis of ambiguous information in order to correct for the negative influence of social comparison.\n\nIn addition, this finding contradicts an alternative explanation that our effects are the result of positive moods inducing heuristic processing and negative moods inducing systematic processing. If heuristic processing were responsible for how participants responded to the comparisons, we would expect the same level of processing of both upward and downward comparisons, with symmetric contrast (or assimilation) to both types of targets. However, positive moods led to the use of a trivial similarity cue to indicate similarity in the upward comparison condition but not in the downward comparison conditions. In addition, if heuristic processing were responsible for the effects in the positive mood conditions, then inducing cognitive load should not have eliminated the self-serving pattern.\n\nThird, we found asymmetry only under positive mood, not under negative mood. If self-serving responses were only defensive, we might have found that negative mood, an aversive state, would have led to an interpretation of information that allowed for recovery. Alternatively, if responses resulted from mood-congruent information search and processing, we would expect that negative mood should lead to asymmetrically negative responses. Instead, negative mood was associated with processing of information with greater neutrality, objectivity, and focus on the data at hand, regardless of the consequence for self-evaluations (for reviews see Bless [2001]; Martin and Clore [2001]).\n\nFinally, the results of the present studies suggest that asymmetric responses are not a result of using mood as a resource (Trope et al. [2001]). According to this model, a positive mood can be a treated as resource to be expended in the pursuit of accurate information. If this were true, in this case, we would have expected that positive mood would have been associated with contrastive responses to comparison targets, a response that is associated with information-seeking motives (Stapel and Koomen [2001a]). Indeed, in other research, the experience of self-affirmation is related to just such symmetric responses to comparisons (Johnson and Stapel, in press).\n\nIn sum, these findings support the growing body of literature showing that positive moods can create an upward spiral (Fredrickson and Joiner [2002]). Numerous cognitive processes are associated with positive mood and in responding to social comparison information; among these the ability to make fine distinctions between distinctive similarity and general similarity may be particularly helpful. Individuals in a positive mood were able to convert what could be considered negative feedback (one is less attractive than another person) into positive self-evaluations. Positive mood granted individuals the ability to see a shared-birthday or a shared-artistic preference as meaningful indicators of shared distinctiveness and similarity, allowing them to assimilate to upward comparison targets. Positive mood also granted individuals the ability to recognize a shared-birthday a meaningless indicator of similarity, and allowed them to contrast with downward comparison targets.\n\nFuture research might investigate how dispositional happiness might be related to the self-serving bias presented here. If positive emotions do create an upward spiral, consistently interpreting ambiguity in self-serving ways might one way in which dispostionally happy people are able to reap self-evaluative boosts from downward comparisons and are buffered from the self-depreciating effects of upward comparisons (Lyubomirsky and Ross [1997]).\n\n## Conclusions\nIt has become increasingly clear that while social comparisons may be ubiquitous, the impact of social comparison information is highly dependent upon the contexts within which comparisons arise and the motivations of the individuals involved. The present studies add to the existing literature by highlighting how mood can influence how individuals treat similarity cues in their environment, such as social comparison information. In the presence of a positive mood, ambiguous social comparison information is interpreted in a self-serving manner, such that positive self-evaluations result. Thus, a good mood can beget not only a good mood, but also beget a more positive self-image.",

content.text: I have what I need. Both impossibility findings survive re-verification against R ground truth and hold under the alternative scale reading; the duplication observation does not survive tool checking and I've graded it accordingly.

headline.statement: Experiment 4's control condition is reported as M = 4.20, SD = .21 on a single whole-number 1-7 rating, and no set of whole-number responses can produce that pair at any sample size -- yet it is the baseline every one of that experiment's eight results is measured against.
headline.evidence: "Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found" and, in the next section, "Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21)". The measure is stated as a single item: "Participants also rated their own attractiveness (How attractive are you?) on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)" (Experiment 1), and Experiment 4 states participants "completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2". For integer responses averaging exactly 4.20, the smallest attainable SD is approximately 0.41.
headline.plain: Experiment 4 says its comparison group averaged 4.20 out of 7 on a single whole-number rating, with the responses spread by only 0.21 around that average -- but whole numbers cannot cluster that tightly around 4.20, because the closest they can get is a spread of about 0.41, roughly twice as wide. The baseline that all eight of that experiment's results are measured against therefore cannot be a real set of answers from real people.

findings.title: Control-condition mean and SD in Experiment 4 unreconstructable from any whole-number sample
findings.location: Experiment 4, 'No load conditions' and 'Cognitive load conditions' (the same control statistics printed twice)
findings.reported: M = 4.20, SD = .21 for the no-mood, no-comparison, no-load hanging control, on the single-item seven-point self-attractiveness rating carried over from Experiments 1 and 2.
findings.computed: SPRITE returns no_solution_proven at n = 15 and n = 30; the sweep additionally proved infeasibility at n = 20 and n = 60. R's rsprite2 independently returns infeasible=true, and does so even when the scale is widened to 1-9, so the result does not depend on the scale bound at all. At n = 15 the only whole-number total consistent with a mean of 4.20 is 63, and no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity falls in the window [265.19, 265.25] implied by SD = 0.21. The smallest SD attainable for an integer mean of exactly 4.20 is approximately 0.41.
findings.assumptions: That the self-evaluation measure is the single whole-number item the paper describes ('How attractive are you?'), which Experiment 4 states by explicit cross-reference to Experiments 1 and 2. The control group's size is not printed; the finding does not depend on it, having been tested at four values. No scale bound is required.

consequence.explanation: All eight of Experiment 4's self-evaluation contrasts are tested against this control mean, so the paper's mechanistic conclusion -- that cognitive load abolishes self-serving reinterpretation -- is computed against a baseline that cannot exist.

findings.plain: The comparison group in the fourth experiment is described as averaging 4.20 out of 7 with the individual answers falling within about 0.21 of that. Since people could only pick whole numbers, their answers cannot bunch that tightly around 4.20; the tightest possible is roughly double. Two separate pieces of software, one of them the standard published tool for this check, agree that no group of people answering that question could have produced these two numbers. Every result in that experiment is stated as a comparison against this group.

findings.title: Two Table 2 self-evaluation cells impossible at the cell size the paper's own design fixes
findings.location: Table 2, Self-evaluation row, Positive/Unambiguous/Upward and Positive/Unambiguous/Downward columns (Experiment 3)
findings.reported: 6.58 (.52) and 4.08 (.52), among eight cells of twelve participants each.
findings.computed: GRIMMER returns impossible for both cells at n = 12. Both means pass the granularity check (candidate integer totals 79 and 49 respectively), so the failure is in the SD: no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity yields an SD rounding to 0.52. Re-run at scale 1-9 as well as 1-7, both cells remain impossible, so the finding survives the alternative scale reading Experiment 3 raises elsewhere. The sweep independently confirmed both with R's rsprite2. Denominator: 24 checks over the eight self-evaluation cells produced 4 impossible results and 20 consistent ones.
findings.assumptions: That the cell size is 12. This is fixed rather than inferred: the paper states N = 96, states a balanced 2x2x2 design, and reports df_error = 88, which is 96 minus 8 cells. That the self-evaluation item is a single whole-number rating, which the paper states by cross-reference. No scale bound is needed -- the result holds at both 1-7 and 1-9.

consequence.explanation: Both cells sit in the unambiguous-cue condition that Experiment 3 uses as its comparison baseline for the claim that self-serving responding requires ambiguity.

findings.plain: Two of the eight groups in the third experiment report averages and spreads that no twelve people answering a whole-number question could have produced. Unlike most such checks, the group size here is not a guess -- the paper's stated total of 96 people split evenly across eight groups fixes it at twelve. These two groups are the comparison condition for that experiment's central claim, that the effect only appears when the information is ambiguous.

findings.title: Experiment 3 target-attractiveness mean of 7.33 above the seven-point maximum the paper cross-references
findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check
findings.reported: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001"
findings.computed: GRIM with bound_source=stated returns failure_mode 'out_of_range': the granularity is fine (352/48 = 7.3333 rounds back to 7.33) but the implied total of 352 exceeds the maximum possible total of 336 for 48 whole-number responses on a 1-7 scale. No sample size rescues it. Separately, rivets_anova confirms the reported F of 170.34 is internally consistent with the two printed means and SDs -- so the F reconciles with a number that cannot be a mean of the stated scale.
findings.assumptions: Downgraded from the sweep's 'impossible' deliberately. The seven-point bound reaches Experiment 3 only by cross-reference -- 'rated their own attractiveness (on the seam [same] measures used in Experiments 1 and 2)', where both those experiments define a seven-point target-attractiveness scale. Two things weaken a hard call: the target-rating sentence that follows does not restate the scale, and the immediately preceding paragraph reports the mood check as M = 7.33 as well, so a nine-point reading would reconcile both values at once. Either the mean is wrong or the description of the scale is wrong; the arithmetic cannot say which.

consequence.explanation: Affects Experiment 3's direction-of-comparison manipulation check, which licenses reading the whole experiment as an upward-versus-downward comparison; the check is significant under either reading of the scale.

findings.plain: Experiment 3 reports an average rating of 7.33 on what it describes as a scale running from 1 to 7 -- an average cannot exceed the top of its own scale. The most likely innocent explanation is that this experiment actually used a nine-point scale and the methods section describes it wrongly, which would also explain the identical value 7.33 reported two sentences earlier for a different measure. Either way, one of the two statements is incorrect, and the paper does not say which.

findings.title: Six Experiment 4 cell means unreconstructable at both candidate cell sizes
findings.location: Experiment 4, 'No load conditions' and 'Cognitive load conditions' (prose cell statistics)
findings.computed: GRIMMER over the eight cells returns 19 impossible of 24 checks at n = 15 and 20 of 24 at n = 14; six cells fail at both candidate sizes. Two further cells, 5.71 (.83) and 3.33 (1.05), pass at one size only.
findings.assumptions: Cell size is derived, not printed. It rests on a factorial N of 118 implied by df_error = 110 across eight cells, giving 14 or 15 per cell. That derived N is itself contradicted by the paper's stated N = 193 (see the sample-size finding), and the two cannot both be right. If the true cells held roughly 22-23 participants, this check would have far less power and these values might be reconstructable. The finding is therefore conditional on the reported degrees of freedom being correct.

consequence.explanation: These six cells carry the whole of Experiment 4's cognitive-load moderation claim, the paper's mechanistic conclusion.

findings.plain: Six of the eight group averages in the fourth experiment cannot be produced by any set of whole-number answers, at either of the two group sizes the paper's own statistics imply. This check is less certain than the others because the paper never prints how many people were in each group -- the sizes had to be worked back from the analysis, and those workings conflict with the total the paper states. If the groups were substantially larger than they appear, some of these averages could be genuine.

findings.title: Four further single-item cell means unreconstructable at both candidate cell sizes in Experiments 1 and 2
findings.location: Table 1, Self-evaluation row (Experiment 2), three cells; and Experiment 1, Self-evaluations, shared-birthday/upward cell
findings.reported: Table 1: 3.17 (.98), 3.07 (.62) and 5.35 (.70). Experiment 1: "asymmetric assimilation towards the upward comparison target (M = 5.08, SD = .52)".
findings.computed: For Table 1, GRIMMER over the eight cells returns 18 impossible of 24 checks at n = 16 and 13 of 24 at n = 15; three cells fail at both. For Experiment 1, SPRITE returns no_solution_proven at n = 12 and GRIM failure at n = 11, so the pair is unreconstructable at both; R's rsprite2 independently returns infeasible=true at n = 12.
findings.assumptions: Neither experiment prints cell sizes. Experiment 2's factorial N of 126 is implied by df_error = 118 across eight cells and reconciles exactly with the stated N = 141 once the df-implied control of 15 is added, giving cells of 15 or 16. Experiment 1's N = 47 across four cells (df_error = 43 confirms four) gives 11 or 12. Only cells failing under both candidates are reported. A markedly unbalanced allocation, which the paper does not report, would weaken these results.

consequence.explanation: The Experiment 1 cell is the one carrying that experiment's headline claim of assimilation to an upward target under a shared-birthday cue, and two of the three Table 1 cells carry Experiment 2's claim that negative mood produces symmetric contrast.

findings.plain: Four more group averages, in the first two experiments, cannot have come from whole-number answers at either group size the paper's statistics allow. One of them is the single result on which the first experiment's main conclusion rests. As with the fourth experiment, the group sizes had to be reconstructed because the paper never prints them, so these are strong signals rather than certainties.

findings.title: Experiment 4's claim of an identical response pattern contradicted by the means printed in the same sentence
findings.location: Experiment 4, Cognitive load conditions
findings.reported: "upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.71, SD = .83) ... and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 3.09, SD = .94) ... This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05) ... and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), relative to the control condition." The control mean is 4.20.
findings.computed: No forensic tool covers a contradiction between prose and the numbers beside it; this is a direct reading of four printed means against the printed control mean of 4.20. The value called 'more positive' than the 4.20 control is 3.33, which is lower; the value called 'less positive' is 5.53, which is higher. The two conditions the paper calls identical are exactly inverted: positive-mood-under-load runs 5.71 up / 3.09 down, neutral-mood-under-load runs 3.33 up / 5.53 down. The three parallel comparisons elsewhere in Experiment 4 (positive no-load 5.64/5.15, neutral no-load 5.47/3.24, positive load 5.71/3.09) all describe their means correctly, so this is not a labelling convention.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The sweep confirmed the sentence reads identically in the XML and in the PDF version of record, so it is not an extraction artefact.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this is a direct reading of four printed means (5.71, 3.09, 3.33, 5.53) against the printed control mean of 4.20 and the sentence describing them. No forensic tool evaluates a text-versus-number direction contradiction.

consequence.explanation: Experiment 4's mechanistic conclusion is that cognitive load makes positive-mood participants behave like neutral-mood participants; the printed means make those two conditions opposite rather than identical.

findings.plain: The fourth experiment's key conclusion is that when people are mentally taxed, those in a good mood stop responding self-servingly and start behaving like everyone else. The sentence stating this describes two groups as showing an identical pattern -- but the numbers printed inside that same sentence show the opposite patterns, each one described backwards relative to the comparison group's score of 4.20. Two numbers appear to have been swapped. Until the authors say which is correct, the experiment's conclusion is not supported by the numbers offered for it.

findings.title: Sixty of Experiment 4's stated 193 participants absent from every analysis it reports
findings.location: Experiment 4, Participants and design, versus Results and discussion
findings.reported: "University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation." The factorial ANOVA reports df_error = 110 and the contrasts against the control report df_error = 124.
findings.computed: check_summation with tolerance 0: df_error = 110 across eight factorial cells implies 118 participants; df_error = 124 across nine groups implies 133 in total, leaving a control of 15. 118 + 15 = 133, against a stated 193 -- a shortfall of 60. The paper reports no exclusions, attrition or missing data. The same arithmetic reconciles exactly for the other four studies: pilot 42+3 = 45, Experiment 1 43+4 = 47, Experiment 2 126+15 = 141, Experiment 3 eight cells of 12 = 96.
findings.assumptions: That the reported degrees of freedom correspond to the models the paper describes, which they do in all four other studies. None beyond the paper's own statements.
findings.reproduction: metascience summation-batch --rows '[{"values":[118,15],"expected_sum":193,"decimals":0,"decimals_total":0,"tolerance":0,"description":"Experiment 4 df-implied N vs stated N"}]'

consequence.explanation: Roughly a third of Experiment 4's stated sample is unaccounted for in every analysis it reports, and the ambiguity also blocks verification of that experiment's cell statistics.

findings.plain: Experiment 4 says 193 people took part, but the statistics it reports only account for about 133 of them. No dropouts, exclusions or missing data are mentioned anywhere. The other four studies in the paper add up exactly, which is what makes this one stand out rather than looking like a house style. It also means nobody can check that experiment's group averages, because the group sizes depend on which of the two totals is right.

findings.title: Pilot mood ANOVA F below every value its own group statistics permit
findings.location: Pilot study, paragraph 2
findings.reported: "the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001", with group means 7.20, 6.15 and 4.98 and SDs .93, .52 and .98.
findings.computed: RIVETS one-way ANOVA over the rounding intervals of the printed means and SDs gives an achievable F range of [26.01, 26.98] at equal allocation, with the reported 18.44 outside it and zero Monte Carlo hits in 5000 samples. The sweep tested two lopsided allocations as well, 10/25/10 and 19/7/19, giving ranges [22.20, 23.07] and [28.03, 29.05]; the reported F is below all three.
findings.assumptions: Group sizes are not stated. This is a genuine one-way ANOVA on three groups -- df(2, 42) matches N = 45 exactly -- so unlike Experiment 2's manipulation check there is no factorial-residual explanation available. Graded suspicious rather than higher because some extreme unequal allocation not tested might reconcile it, and because the significance decision is unaffected. The tool itself returned highly_suspicious; the downgrade is mine.

consequence.explanation: Affects the pilot's demonstration that the mood induction worked; the reported F is smaller than the group statistics imply, so the conclusion of a significant effect stands.

findings.plain: The pilot study's test statistic is smaller than the group averages and spreads printed beside it can produce, under equal group sizes and two unequal ones. The effect it reports would have been larger, not smaller, so this does not change the conclusion that the mood manipulation worked -- but the number does not follow from the numbers given for it.

findings.title: Two dependent measures named in Table 1's caption reported nowhere in Experiment 2
findings.location: Table 1 caption versus Table 1 body and Experiment 2 text
findings.reported: The caption promises "effects ... on self-evaluations, ratings of target similarity, and use of information to benefit the self". The table contains exactly one data row, Self-evaluation.
findings.computed: Table 1 returns one data row of eight cells in both the XML grid and, per the sweep, the PDF. Neither 'ratings of target similarity' nor 'use of information to benefit the self' appears anywhere in Experiment 2's text or table, and Experiment 2's Dependent measures section never describes a similarity measure, although Experiment 3 does.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This may be a caption inherited from a fuller table that was cut, rather than measures collected and suppressed; the paper gives no way to tell.

consequence.explanation: Two dependent measures named in the table's own caption are never reported in Experiment 2, so their results cannot be evaluated at all.

findings.plain: The title above Table 1 says it shows results for three different measures. The table shows one. The other two -- how similar participants rated the comparison person, and whether they used the information to their own benefit -- appear nowhere in that experiment. Either they were measured and not reported, or the table's title was left over from an earlier version.

findings.title: Data-availability offer with no data deposited
findings.location: Experiment 3, footnote 4
findings.reported: "Complete data and results available from the first author."
findings.computed: No supplementary files accompany the record; nothing could be read. Two dependent measures named in Table 1's caption are also never reported.
findings.assumptions: This records the presence of an availability claim and the absence of deposited data. It is not evidence about the authors' willingness to supply data on request, which was not tested.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this records the presence of a data-availability claim in the text and the absence of any deposited data file alongside the article. No forensic tool evaluates it.

consequence.explanation: Every impossibility recorded above could be settled immediately by the raw data this footnote offers; none of it is deposited, and the offer is attached to one footnote in one experiment rather than to the paper.

findings.plain: A footnote in the third experiment says complete data are available from the first author, but no data accompany the article. Every one of the arithmetic problems in this review could be resolved -- in either direction -- by seeing the actual responses.

findings.title: Two degrees-of-freedom values inconsistent with the designs they are attributed to
findings.location: Experiment 1, Self-evaluations; and Experiment 3, Perceptions of similarity
findings.reported: Experiment 1: "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" for a simple effect, where every other test in that experiment uses df_error = 43. Experiment 3: three correlations reported as r(24), e.g. "r(24) = .87, p < .001".
findings.computed: For Experiment 1, N = 47 in a 2x2 design gives df_error = 43; the printed 46 equals N - 1 and corresponds to no error term in the stated design. The p-value is unaffected: F(1,46) = 6.95 gives p = .0114 and F(1,43) = 6.95 gives p = .0116, both printing as .011. For Experiment 3, each correlation is computed within one mood-by-ambiguity combination spanning two cells of twelve, so 24 participants and df = 22; the printed df = 24 implies n = 26.
findings.assumptions: That the correlations were computed within a single mood-by-ambiguity combination, which is how the text describes them. The Experiment 3 discrepancy could be a convention slip of reporting n rather than n - 2.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: these compare printed degrees-of-freedom values against the sample sizes implied by the stated designs, which no forensic tool evaluates.

consequence.explanation: Affects Experiment 1's symmetric-contrast simple effect and the three Experiment 3 correlations used to argue similarity ratings mediate the effect; no significance decision changes.

findings.plain: Two places in the paper report a technical number that describes how many people went into a test, and in both cases it does not match the design described. Neither changes whether the result is statistically significant, but both suggest the analyses were not all run on the samples the paper describes.

findings.title: Three of sixty-five reported test statistics inconsistent with their own p-values
findings.location: Whole body text (Pilot and Experiments 1-4)
findings.computed: statcheck over all 65 NHST results recomputes p = .2237, .6061 and .0054 respectively; zero decision errors. Two have benign explanations: rivets_anova independently confirms the pilot F of .27 reconciles with its group statistics and yields p = .757 once the numerator df is read as 2 rather than 1, which the three-group design requires; and .83 for F = 1.50 may be a transposition of .23. The paper also prints two malformed p-values, 'p = 011' and 'p = 001', normalised to .011 and .001 for the run.
findings.assumptions: Three out of sixty-five is a low rate and unremarkable on its own -- roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such mismatch. Reported for completeness rather than as a substantive charge.

consequence.explanation: None of the three inconsistencies crosses the paper's significance threshold, so no reported conclusion changes.

findings.plain: Three of the paper's sixty-five statistical results do not match the probability values printed beside them. This is an ordinary rate of typographical slippage -- about half of error-free papers have at least one -- and none of the three changes whether a result counts as significant. It is recorded so the reader knows it was checked, not as a criticism.

findings.title: Repeated summary values across independent samples, below the threshold at which duplication checking flags them
findings.location: Pilot study versus Table 1 (Experiment 2); Experiment 3 Manipulation check; Table 2 Similarity row
findings.reported: The pilot's three mood-condition SDs are .93, .52 and .98; Table 1's first three self-evaluation SDs are .93, .52 and .98, in the same order. Separately: two attractiveness SDs identical at 1.19 in one sentence; two Table 2 similarity means identical at 6.81; two pilot self-evaluation means identical at 6.98; the value 7.33 reported for two different Experiment 3 measures; and the control mean of exactly 4.20 in both Experiment 2 and Experiment 4.
findings.computed: detect_duplication over 1407 cross-source comparisons of 58 (mean, SD) cells found zero identical pairs between independent samples; three flagged items were digit transpositions between 5.35 and 5.53, which is weak. Re-run in stage 2 on the pilot and Table 1 blocks specifically, it again returned consistent with zero identical pairs, because it matches mean-and-SD together and only the SDs coincide. The SD-sequence observation therefore has NO tool backing and is recorded as a reading.
findings.assumptions: Repeated values are ordinary in small samples and prove nothing on their own (rulebook rule 8). The pilot and Experiment 2 involve different participants and different measures on different scales -- a four-item nine-point composite versus a single seven-point item -- which is what makes three SDs coinciding in sequence worth noting, but I could not quantify how improbable it is with any validated tool.
findings.reproduction: metascience duplication-detect --blocks '[{"label":"Pilot mood by condition","sample_id":"pilot","independent":true,"cells":[{"label":"positive","value":7.2,"sd":0.93},{"label":"control","value":6.15,"sd":0.52},{"label":"negative","value":4.98,"sd":0.98}]},{"label":"Exp 2 Table 1 first three cells","sample_id":"exp2","independent":true,"cells":[{"label":"pos/same/up","value":5.25,"sd":0.93},{"label":"pos/same/down","value":5.53,"sd":0.52},{"label":"pos/diff/up","value":3.17,"sd":0.98}]}]' --decimals-mean 2 --decimals-sd 2

consequence.explanation: No claim depends on this; it is recorded as a weak corroborating pattern and as a record of what duplication checking ruled out.

findings.plain: Several numbers recur across studies that used different people and different questionnaires -- most noticeably, the three spread values from the pilot study reappear in the same order in the first three columns of Experiment 2's table. The automated check for copied statistics found nothing, because it looks for averages and spreads matching together and here only the spreads match. This is an observation, not a finding: repeated values happen by chance, and I could not measure how likely this particular coincidence is.

not_checked.reason: The similarity index is a mean of three nine-point items, so it moves in steps of 1/(3n) rather than 1/n, and the granularity tools have no items parameter. Running them with 1/n would manufacture impossibilities, and hand-checking the 1/36 granularity would be unvalidated arithmetic.

## What the paper claims

A pilot study and four between-subjects experiments argue that positive mood lets people reinterpret ambiguous similarity information in whatever direction flatters them: assimilating towards more attractive comparison targets and contrasting away from less attractive ones. Experiment 1 establishes the asymmetry using a shared-birthday cue; Experiment 2 rules out a mood-congruency explanation by showing negative mood does not produce it; Experiment 3 shows the effect requires the similarity cue to be ambiguous; Experiment 4 shows it is abolished by cognitive load, which is the mechanistic conclusion the paper builds towards. Self-evaluation is throughout a single whole-number rating, "How attractive are you?", on a seven-point scale.

## A note on the record, and why it changes nothing here

The article is published as retracted, and the second author's corpus was retracted following the 2011 Levelt, Noort and Drenth investigations. No finding in this review rests on that. Every result below was derived from the printed numbers, and each names whether it depends on a sample size the paper states or one that had to be worked backwards from reported degrees of freedom. The arithmetic was checkable without knowing how the story ended.

## Why the impossibility findings carry the weight they do

Because self-evaluation is a single whole-number item, the printed means and standard deviations are heavily constrained: only certain combinations can arise from any set of responses at all. Two of the paper's combinations cannot arise from any set.

The stronger of the two is Experiment 4's control condition, printed twice as M = 4.20, SD = .21. Whole numbers averaging exactly 4.20 must sit at least as far apart as a mix of 4s and 5s allows, which forces a standard deviation of roughly 0.41 or more. This holds at every sample size, and it does not depend on the scale at all -- I re-ran it at 1-9 as well as 1-7, and against R's `rsprite2`, which is the published reference implementation. Both engines agree no such sample exists. The immediate contrast is Experiment 2's control condition, M = 4.20, SD = .86, which reconstructs cleanly at n = 15. That is the control on the method: the same check, the same scale, the same nominal mean, and one passes.

The second is Table 2. Two cells in the unambiguous-cue condition of Experiment 3, 6.58 (.52) and 4.08 (.52), admit no whole-number sample at twelve per cell -- and twelve is not a guess here. The paper states N = 96, states a balanced 2x2x2 design, and reports df_error = 88, which is 96 minus 8. I re-ran both cells at 1-9 as well as 1-7 in case Experiment 3 used a wider scale than the methods describe, and they fail either way.

Ten further cells across Experiments 1, 2 and 4 fail the same checks, but only at cell sizes reconstructed from degrees of freedom rather than stated. Those are reported one grade lower for that reason, and Experiment 4's are lower again in confidence, because the degrees of freedom they rest on contradict that experiment's own stated N.

## What I dropped or softened from the numeric sweep

Four sweep findings I did not carry forward as defects. The sweep had already downgraded Experiment 2's manipulation-check F of 716.92 to indeterminate, correctly: the tool recomputes a one-way ANOVA while the paper's df_error of 118 comes from the full factorial residual, which accounts for nearly all of the apparent gap. The XML-versus-PDF reconciliation is a gap in our extraction tooling -- the XML dropped Table 1's footnote -- and belongs in limitations, not against the authors. The duplication sweep and the multiplicity check are negative results and are recorded as such: across 1407 comparisons there is not one identical mean-and-SD pair between independent samples, and no Experiment 4 claim is lost to correction for multiple testing. Whatever is wrong here, wholesale copy-paste and undisclosed multiplicity are not it.

Two I softened. The Experiment 3 mean of 7.33 on a stated seven-point scale is graded highly_suspicious rather than impossible: the seven-point bound reaches Experiment 3 only by cross-reference, and the same paragraph reports the mood check at 7.33 too, so a nine-point scale would reconcile both at once. Either the mean or the methods description is wrong; the arithmetic cannot say which, and a finding this contingent should not lead a review. The pilot ANOVA I kept at suspicious rather than the tool's own highly_suspicious, because group sizes are unstated and some extreme allocation I did not test might reconcile it.

One I have handled more carefully than the sweep did. The pilot's three mood SDs -- .93, .52, .98 -- reappear in that exact order as the first three SDs of Table 1, in a different experiment, on different participants, measuring something else on a different scale. The duplication tool does not flag this, because it matches means and SDs together and here only the SDs coincide. I ran it again specifically on those two blocks and it returned nothing. So this is a reading with no tool behind it, and it is recorded at indeterminate. It is not evidence; it is a thing worth asking about.

## The reasoning the sweep could not do

Experiment 4 contradicts itself in the sentence carrying its conclusion. The paper's mechanistic claim is that load makes positive-mood participants behave like neutral-mood ones. The printed means make those two conditions opposite: positive-under-load runs 5.71 upward and 3.09 downward against a control of 4.20, while neutral-under-load runs 3.33 upward and 5.53 downward -- each described backwards relative to the control, in a paragraph that then calls the patterns identical. The three parallel comparisons elsewhere in the same experiment get the arithmetic right, so this is not a labelling convention. Two numbers look transposed. Until that is confirmed, the experiment's conclusion is unsupported by the numbers offered for it -- and it sits on top of a control condition that cannot exist and a sample sixty participants short of the one stated.

Around this: a footnote offers complete data that are not deposited, and Table 1's caption names two dependent measures that appear nowhere in Experiment 2. Both are recoverable by the authors in an afternoon.

Verification coverage was broad -- all 65 reported test statistics, all 24 table cells, and both reported sample-flow reconciliations -- and most of it passed.

## Trust verdict

The two experiments carrying the paper's central mechanistic claims each report at least one summary statistic that no dataset could have produced, and Experiment 4 additionally contradicts its own conclusion and cannot account for a third of its stated sample. I have no confidence in the accuracy of the reported statistics, and the results should not be relied upon without the raw data.

headline.statement: Experiment 4's control condition is reported as M = 4.20, SD = .21 on a single whole-number 1-7 rating, and no set of whole-number responses can produce that pair at any sample size -- yet it is the baseline every one of that experiment's eight results is measured against.
headline.evidence: "Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found" and, in the next section, "Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21)". The measure is stated as a single item: "Participants also rated their own attractiveness (How attractive are you?) on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)" (Experiment 1), and Experiment 4 states participants "completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2". For integer responses averaging exactly 4.20, the smallest attainable SD is approximately 0.41.
headline.plain: Experiment 4 says its comparison group averaged 4.20 out of 7 on a single whole-number rating, with the responses spread by only 0.21 around that average -- but whole numbers cannot cluster that tightly around 4.20, because the closest they can get is a spread of about 0.41, roughly twice as wide. The baseline that all eight of that experiment's results are measured against therefore cannot be a real set of answers from real people.

findings.title: Control-condition mean and SD in Experiment 4 unreconstructable from any whole-number sample
findings.location: Experiment 4, 'No load conditions' and 'Cognitive load conditions' (the same control statistics printed twice)
findings.reported: M = 4.20, SD = .21 for the no-mood, no-comparison, no-load hanging control, on the single-item seven-point self-attractiveness rating carried over from Experiments 1 and 2.
findings.computed: SPRITE returns no_solution_proven at n = 15 and n = 30; the sweep additionally proved infeasibility at n = 20 and n = 60. R's rsprite2 independently returns infeasible=true, and does so even when the scale is widened to 1-9, so the result does not depend on the scale bound at all. At n = 15 the only whole-number total consistent with a mean of 4.20 is 63, and no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity falls in the window [265.19, 265.25] implied by SD = 0.21. The smallest SD attainable for an integer mean of exactly 4.20 is approximately 0.41.
findings.assumptions: That the self-evaluation measure is the single whole-number item the paper describes ('How attractive are you?'), which Experiment 4 states by explicit cross-reference to Experiments 1 and 2. The control group's size is not printed; the finding does not depend on it, having been tested at four values. No scale bound is required.

consequence.explanation: All eight of Experiment 4's self-evaluation contrasts are tested against this control mean, so the paper's mechanistic conclusion -- that cognitive load abolishes self-serving reinterpretation -- is computed against a baseline that cannot exist.

findings.plain: The comparison group in the fourth experiment is described as averaging 4.20 out of 7 with the individual answers falling within about 0.21 of that. Since people could only pick whole numbers, their answers cannot bunch that tightly around 4.20; the tightest possible is roughly double. Two separate pieces of software, one of them the standard published tool for this check, agree that no group of people answering that question could have produced these two numbers. Every result in that experiment is stated as a comparison against this group.

findings.reported: 6.58 (.52) and 4.08 (.52), among eight cells of twelve participants each.
findings.computed: GRIMMER returns impossible for both cells at n = 12. Both means pass the granularity check (candidate integer totals 79 and 49 respectively), so the failure is in the SD: no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity yields an SD rounding to 0.52. Re-run at scale 1-9 as well as 1-7, both cells remain impossible, so the finding survives the alternative scale reading Experiment 3 raises elsewhere. The sweep independently confirmed both with R's rsprite2. Denominator: 24 checks over the eight self-evaluation cells produced 4 impossible results and 20 consistent ones.
findings.assumptions: That the cell size is 12. This is fixed rather than inferred: the paper states N = 96, states a balanced 2x2x2 design, and reports df_error = 88, which is 96 minus 8 cells. That the self-evaluation item is a single whole-number rating, which the paper states by cross-reference. No scale bound is needed -- the result holds at both 1-7 and 1-9.

consequence.explanation: Both cells sit in the unambiguous-cue condition that Experiment 3 uses as its comparison baseline for the claim that self-serving responding requires ambiguity.

findings.plain: Two of the eight groups in the third experiment report averages and spreads that no twelve people answering a whole-number question could have produced. Unlike most such checks, the group size here is not a guess -- the paper's stated total of 96 people split evenly across eight groups fixes it at twelve. These two groups are the comparison condition for that experiment's central claim, that the effect only appears when the information is ambiguous.

findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check
findings.reported: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001"
findings.computed: GRIM with bound_source=stated returns failure_mode 'out_of_range': the granularity is fine (352/48 = 7.3333 rounds back to 7.33) but the implied total of 352 exceeds the maximum possible total of 336 for 48 whole-number responses on a 1-7 scale.
